. The rising volatility and increasing strategic importance of the Arctic has long been acknowledged, but in 2024, competition in the region became even more pitched. On 24 July, the North American Aerospace Defense Command intercepted a Russian and a Chinese military aircraft operating in the Alaska air defense identification zone in the Arctic. In early October, two Russian Border Guard ships and two Chinese Coast Guard ships conducted a joint maritime patrol approximately 440 miles southwest of St. Lawrence Island in the Bering Sea. These first-ever joint Russian and Chinese deployments show how far the geopolitical dynamics in the Arctic region have already shifted and why the U.S. must respond decisively. The climate of the Arctic strategic environment has changed; it is heating up, both literally and figuratively.

. Challenges posed by Russia and China Over the past decade, Russia has reestablished 14 Cold War–era Arctic military bases and launched icebreaking warships. It held a massive naval exercise in the Bering Sea that displaced American fishing vessels working in the U.S. exclusive economic zone and continued its posturing through military exercises that have included antiship cruise missiles fired from submarines. Russia has never stopped making expansive and unsupported claims on Arctic resources. A Russian politician recently floated the idea of seizing Alaska as retaliation for U.S. sanctions. The conflict in Ukraine shows Russia’s ability to commit to a losing cause, almost certainly because the country Russia is invading, in that case, is deeply engrained in Putin’s sense of Russian national identity. The Arctic would almost certainly fall into the same broad category. For its part, China in 2020 launched its first domestically built icebreaker and recently announced intentions to build a nuclear-powered icebreaker. As China and Russia continue to explore the depths of their “friendship without limits,” their collaboration in the Arctic domain is inevitable and only heightens the threat to U.S. interests.

. The State Department recognized the Arctic’s growing strategic importance when it nominated Michael Sfraga as the first-ever ambassador at large for the Arctic region. DoD did the same when it established the Ted Stevens Center for Arctic Security Studies and the office of Arctic and Global Resilience Office at the Pentagon, led by a new a Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense. The first deputy assistant secretary who served in this position, Iris Ferguson, summed up the problem succinctly: “There might not be conflict now—and there hopefully will never be conflict in the Arctic—but we need to be prepared to operate there.” Environmental Changes and Strategic Implications Threats from major strategic competitors are not the only challenges facing the United States and its allies in the Arctic. Rapid environmental change invites new resource exploitation and probing foreign-government activity, both of which threaten U.S. sovereignty along its newly exposed fourth coast. The Arctic holds significant portions of the world’s rare-earth minerals, in addition to vast untapped oil and natural gas reserves. Scientists are tracking the northward migration of fish stocks into the increasingly ice-free waters of the Arctic. Global distant-water fishing fleets—especially those led by China and defended by the China Coast Guard—will not be far behind. Despite the United States’ December 2023 claim for an Extended Continental Shelf—a provision granted by Article 76 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea—

. As the existing lead federal agency for Arctic operations, the Coast Guard has explored numerous concepts for how to organize staff elements to manage Arctic policy and operations. In 2021, one of the authors, Captain Woityra, had the honor of leading 134 men and women to the northern-most point ever reached by a U.S. surface ship in the winter. The trip was successful, but it exposed inefficiencies and outmoded structures guiding Coast Guard operations in the Arctic. The Coast Guard cannot manage this region alone. In the interest of national security and defense of U.S. sovereign rights in the Arctic, this function must be elevated above a single agency or department. In fall 2023, the Coast Guard tacitly acknowledged C2 seams between the east and west Arctic and the strictly domestic focus of the District 17 (Alaska) Commander. They launched a proof-of-concept effort to enhance and unify C2 for its operations in the Arctic by establishing Coast Guard Task Force (CGTF) Arctic. The Coast Guard Pacific Area Deputy Commander, a two-star rear admiral, has been designated to serve as the task force’s first commander. When tasked and allocated with resources, CGTF Arctic plans, synchronizes, and exercises tactical control of Coast Guard forces for missions in the Arctic. This
Arctic task force concept should be expanded by including allied, joint-force, and whole-of-government capacities. That should be the structure for the ACITF
Experience has shown that the best way to address diverse and asymmetric threats is through a U.S. interagency approach that
aligns efforts with allies and partners
. The interagency task-force model has been used with great success by Joint Interagency Task Force (JIATF) South and JIATF West.

It provides all stakeholders a forum to identify threats, fuse actionable intelligence into operational tasking, project hard or soft/smart power to provide influential presence, and mount an active defense to counter threats

) Given the actions already underway by strategic competitors, and the pace of environmental change and resultant economic activity, the ACITF should be established, staffed, and funded as soon as possible

. The staff should be based in Anchorage, where the Alaskan Command at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson can be combined with the Coast Guard’s proof-of-concept CGTF Arctic. These elements would provide an immediate foundation for the ACITF. This location and the organizational foundation that already exists would place the C2 structure in the same time zone as operational task units. It also would put an Alaskan imprint on the leadership structure responsible for defending U.S. Arctic interests in the state that makes the United States an Arctic nation. Several actions would set up the proposed ACITF establishment for success: 1) The mission must be statutorily defined, and the President’s Unified Command Plan must be updated to reflect the task force’s roles, responsibilities, and authorities to interface with the applicable DoD Geographic Combatant Commands within the Arctic region. 2) As an emerging requirement,

this organization will likely demand new resources. Until such resources can be allocated, the responsibilities, efficiency, and function of other DoD joint, combined, and interagency task forces would be a prudent place to harvest resources to stand up the ACITF

. The mission performance metrics and personnel and funding allocations must build on the lessons learned from many previous Joint and Combined Task Forces. 3) The military threat demands an organization that heeds the tenets of Joint Publication 1, as well as other applicable allied and interagency joint publications. This task force would depend on intergovernmental and international interoperability to succeed. That is why
the ACITF must be a DoD initiative with integral support from the U.S. Coast Guard and the Department of State

. As with JIATF South and JIATF West, heading the organization with a Coast Guard flag officer makes sense. This would acknowledge the Coast Guard’s role as lead federal agency for Arctic operations and leverage the Coast Guard’s Title 10 and Title 14 authorities and missions.
